extracted.intended_audience: mathematics-education researchers, curriculum developers, and elementary/middle-grade practitioners interested in early-algebra interventions and retention
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the design, assessment, and longer-term retention outcomes of a Grades 3–5 early-algebra instructional intervention, and identifying which algebraic ideas and practices persist or fade one year post-intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic thinking practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The intervention and assessments center on the algebraic thinking practices of "generalizing, representing, justifying, and reasoning with mathematical structure and relationships."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices form the basis of curricular framework, instructional tasks, and assessment design; assessments and tasks should elicit evidence of these practices rather than only procedural skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized arithmetic (Big Idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as “generalizing arithmetic relationships, including fundamental properties of number and operation (e.g., the Commutative Property of Addition), and reasoning about the structure of arithmetic expressions rather than their computational value.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students engaging in generalized arithmetic should look across multiple computations, notice underlying structures, and represent/justify/reason about these structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence, expressions, equations, and inequalities (Big Idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes developing a relational understanding of the equal sign, representing and reasoning with expressions and equations in symbolic form, and describing relationships between and among generalized quantities that may or may not be equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment items should probe relational conceptions of the equals sign and the ability to represent and reason with symbolic expressions/equations; beware tasks that only elicit operational 'answer-finding' conceptions of '='.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional thinking (Big Idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Involves generalizing relationships between covarying quantities and representing/reasoning with those relationships through natural language, algebraic notation, tables, and graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks should ask students to identify rules in words and symbols, make far predictions, fill tables from rules, and reason about changes to rules; progression from simple to more complex relationships is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment alignment to big ideas and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments should be designed to measure understanding of the big algebraic ideas and algebraic thinking practices that form the basis of the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study the assessment consisted largely of open-response items that ask students to show their thinking; many items were based on previously validated research items. Use items that elicit explanations, representations, and predictions aligned to targeted big ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-response items and evidence of thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Majority of assessment items are open-response and ask students to show their thinking, enabling scoring for both correctness and strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open-response format allows coders to evaluate not just final answers but strategy use and justification; include multipart items to probe different facets of a single big idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring dimensions: correctness and strategy use
rubrics_metrics.description: Student responses should be coded for correctness as well as strategy use; both were reported to parallel one another in results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coding schemes developed and validated in prior work; report both correctness percentages and strategy-level coding to provide richer evidence of learning and transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind, trained coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses should be coded by trained coders who are unaware of students’ treatment condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain coder blinding to prevent bias; employ established coding schemes (cited sources) and training procedures to ensure reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention dosage and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention delivered as eighteen 1-hour lessons per year in Grades 3–5, taught during regular mathematics instructional time by classroom teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained, repeated exposure across multiple years is a design feature; dosage and integration into regular instruction (not pull-out) are emphasized for ecological validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task design characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional tasks should engage the big algebraic ideas through problem-solving, involve small-group and whole-group discussion, and generally allow for multiple points of entry so students at varying levels can engage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt tasks from research-based sources; ensure multiple access points and opportunities for representation, generalization, and justification to support diverse learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers implementing the intervention participated in monthly professional development to prepare them to teach the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained PD accompanies curriculum implementation to support fidelity and teacher capacity; include PD that models tasks, discussion facilitation, and interpretation of student reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of validated/previously researched items
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment items were largely based on items that had performed well in previous research (e.g., Carpenter et al., Carraher et al., Knuth et al.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage previously validated items to increase comparability across studies and ensure construct validity; document item provenance and prior performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention evaluation constructs: persistence and fadeout
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention studies should frame impacts in terms of persistence (sustained beneficial impacts) and fadeout (dissipation of effects) as constructs for interpreting longer-term outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these constructs to structure research questions and discussion; consider item-level analyses to identify domains of persistence vs. fadeout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of skills likely to persist
rubrics_metrics.description: Bailey et al. (2017) criteria: interventions that sustain impacts tend to target skills that are malleable, fundamental, and would not eventually develop in the absence of the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing interventions, prioritize malleable and fundamental skills (e.g., concepts central to later learning) and measure whether these would otherwise be expected to develop naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustaining environments and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: High-quality postintervention environments and alignment between intervention content and subsequent instruction are critical for sustaining earlier gains; continued practice, relearning, advanced training, or continued exposure facilitate retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for elementary-to-middle (and beyond) alignment of curricular emphases (e.g., functional thinking, equivalence, variable representation); assess the degree to which follow-on instruction calls on intervention-learned knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: SES grouping for subgroup analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A median-split technique can be used to divide elementary schools into high or low SES categories based on percentage of students receiving free or reduced-price lunch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SES grouping as a between-subjects factor in analyses to examine differential effects; report method of grouping and any limitations of median-split approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis methods for retention studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine overall change analyses (e.g., repeated measures ANOVA with treatment and SES as between-subject factors) with item-level tests of change (e.g., McNemar’s test) to examine both aggregate and item-specific persistence/fadeout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report main effects, interactions (e.g., time × treatment), and item-level significance; present both percentage-correct summaries and change in number of item parts correct for practical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and argumentation as measurable targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Argumentation (e.g., producing a general argument that the sum of three odd numbers is odd) and representation-based proofs are valid, measurable targets of early-algebra instruction, though challenging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include tasks that specifically prompt general arguments and representation-based justifications; expect lower baseline proficiency and track change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on multiple roles of variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions should sustain attention to the different roles variables can take (variable as varying quantity, variable as generalized number, variables in relation to one another in a function rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks and assessments that elicit these different variable interpretations; teaching should make distinctions explicit to support later formal algebra learning.
